paras: The attempted lynching of Sylvanus K. Makison took place at Kewanee, Henry County, Illinois, between August 28 and August 31, 1882, when crowds of men tried to seize and hang the farm hand, who was jailed for the murder of Mrs. Maggie Copeland. Officers, citizens and the state's attorney held the crowds back with promises that the law would take its course, and Makison was removed alive to the jail at Cambridge. The case drew wide notice because it coincided with the Kewanee bank robbery and because Makison, after confessing, asked to be handed over to the mob.

On Saturday, August 26, Mrs. Maggie Copeland was found killed at a farm house on John Dustin's farm, three miles south of Kewanee, while the rest of the household was away. According to the first wire report, she had been knocked down with a board, shot twice and struck with a club, and money had been taken that only someone familiar with the house could have found. Sylvanus McKisson, as the dispatch spelled his name, was arrested on suspicion the same day with a revolver that had two empty chambers.

Ohio papers reported that Mrs. Copeland, the daughter of George Frazier, had grown up in Jefferson County, Ohio, and that Makison had come west with the Copelands to find work. The first dispatch predicted that if his guilt were made plain he would 'undoubtedly be lynched before morning, as public feeling is at fever heat.'

On the night of August 28, according to a Kewanee dispatch of the next day, 'an organized body of 100 men' appeared to lynch the prisoner at the lockup. An outbreak was prevented by the assurance of the sheriff and officers of Kewanee that he would be dealt with according to law. Meanwhile a Pinkerton detective, posing as the bank robber Welch, spent the night in his cell, and Makison confessed and showed where he had hidden the stolen money.

A larger crowd gathered on the day of his examination, at which he waived examination and pleaded guilty. An August 30 dispatch put the mob at 500 men who 'attempted to lynch him' that afternoon, while an account from the Cincinnati Enquirer said fully five thousand men filled the streets that morning. Leading citizens and State's Attorney Gilchrist persuaded the crowd to let officers take him to the county jail at Cambridge, about twenty miles away. Several reports said Makison begged the officers to let the crowd hang him, saying he wished to die as soon as possible.

A coroner's inquest was expected to finish on August 30, and Makison was held for trial in the Cambridge jail. No report of an indictment, trial or sentence appears in the coverage, and no one in the crowds was reported arrested.

Only the white press covered the case, mostly through two wire dispatches, the first spreading under headlines such as 'Lynching Probable' from Salt Lake City to St. Paul. The confession and mob story ran in Washington, New York and New Haven papers on August 30 and 31, under headlines including 'A Murderer Anxious to Die', and a later version headed 'Asking to be Hanged' raised the crowd to 5,000. German- and Norwegian-language papers carried it in crime roundups, the Decorah-Posten noting that the crowd yielded to officials' promises.

Papers in the victim's home region of eastern Ohio covered her background and burial, and the Wheeling Register's headline welcomed that 'Better Counsel Prevails.' By contrast, a Chicago letter in the Memphis Public Ledger said 'the fiend Mackisson' and the bank robbers deserved 'a dance at the end of ropes' and that it was time Judge Lynch was called to preside. None of the reports gave the race of Makison or of the Copelands.

Accounts differ on the size and timing of the crowd: 100 men on the night of August 28, 500 men on the afternoon of August 30, or 5,000 men on the morning of the examination or on Thursday afternoon. They also differ on the place of the murder, given as John Dustin's farm or Weathersfield, and on the sum stolen, given as $80 or about $800.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Sylvanus K. Makison
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Crowds of 100 to 5,000 men gathered at Kewanee to hang a jailed murder suspect and were turned back by officers and citizens (A8, A16, A18); no article states the race of anyone involved.

Mobs of 100, 500 or 5,000 men tried to seize and hang Makison for the Copeland murder, which would have been an illegal group killing under a pretext of justice (A8, A16, A18, A21), but the authorities prevented it and he was removed to the county jail alive (A18); this is an attempted lynching.

Separate dispatches of Aug. 29 (A8, A10), Aug. 30 (A16) and the Ohio and Enquirer material in the Wheeling Register (A18) agree that a crowd tried to lynch Makison and was held back, though they differ on its size and timing.

accounts.label: Kewanee wire dispatch, Aug. 29
accounts.gist: Many lynching threats were heard and an organized body of 100 men came the previous night to lynch the prisoner, but the sheriff's and officers' assurances prevented an outbreak.

accounts.label: Kewanee wire dispatch, Aug. 30
accounts.gist: After confessing, Makison faced a mob of 500 men who tried to lynch him that afternoon and were stopped by the authorities; he begged to be handed over.

accounts.label: Cincinnati Enquirer particulars (via Wheeling Register)
accounts.gist: Fully five thousand men filled the streets the morning of the examination, determined to hang him; leading citizens and State's Attorney Gilchrist secured his removal to the Cambridge jail.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wire as crime news, with headlines like 'Lynching Probable' and 'Asking to be Hanged' that treated lynching as an expected outcome.
The Rock Island Argus dispatch credited the 'judicious conduct of the officers and citizens' for preventing violence.
The Wheeling Register's headline said 'Better Counsel Prevails' while assuring readers he would 'pull hemp' legally.
A Chicago letter in the Memphis Public Ledger said 'the fiend Mackisson' deserved 'a dance at the end of ropes' and called for Judge Lynch.

conflicts.note: The 100-man gathering appears to be a separate, earlier episode; the 500 and 5,000 figures describe the crowd at the examination, and the Daily Republican's text otherwise repeats the Aug. 30 wire.
He may have confessed to the detective and then again formally before the examination (A18).

info: Murder of Mrs. Maggie Copeland on Saturday, Aug. 26, 1882; an organized body of 100 men came to lynch the suspect on the night of Aug. 28; a larger crowd tried again at his examination, reported as the afternoon of Aug. 30 (500 men) or Thursday, Aug. 31 (5,000 men).

Murder at a farm house on John Dustin's farm three miles south of Kewanee (also given as four miles from Kewanee, and as Weathersfield); mob gatherings around the Kewanee lockup and in the streets during the examination.
Target of the mob: Sylvanus K. Makison, a farm hand (spelled Makinson, McKisson, Nickisson, McKesson, Mackison, Machinson, Malsinson); race not stated.
Accused of murdering and robbing Mrs. Maggie Copeland; he confessed and, at his examination, waived examination and pleaded guilty.
An 'organized body' of men, later a 'mob'; no names or race given.
No one was killed by the mob; Makison was removed to the jail at Cambridge, about twenty miles away.
